text: I added why central Mughal power weakened after Aurangzeb, next to what is already on your Stage. Historians disagree on whether this was a collapse or a shift of power to regional states.

block.title: Why Mughal power declined
block.because: You asked why the Mughal empire declined

sections.md: After [[Aurangzeb|person]] died in 1707, the emperors in Delhi lost control of most of the empire within a few decades [E]. Long wars in the [[Deccan|place]], rising regional powers such as the [[Marathas|term]], and repeated succession wars drained the treasury and the loyalty of the nobility [L]. Whether this was a collapse or a shift of power to regional states is debated [C].

block.title: Causes and consequences: Mughal decline
block.because: You asked why the Mughal empire declined

nodes.label: Deccan wars drain treasury and army
Jat and Sikh revolts in the north
Aurangzeb dies; princes fight for the throne

edges.why: Aurangzeb went south largely to fight the Marathas.
Long wars added nobles faster than good revenue land could be found for them.
The Deccan campaigns cost money and men the centre could not replace.
How far a shortage of jagirs drove the decline is debated.
Maratha raids and levies cut into Mughal revenue and authority.
Revolts close to the capital forced costly campaigns.
With no settled rule of succession, princes fought and the nobility split.
Short reigns left real power with rival noble factions.
Governors like the Nizam ruled in the emperor’s name but answered to no one.
A weakened centre could not defend the north-west.
With the centre weak, the Company dealt with regional rulers one by one.
British power absorbed what remained; after 1857 the dynasty was ended.

sections.md: Aurangzeb spent his last 25 years campaigning in the Deccan (1681-1707) [E]. Mughal nobles were paid through jagirs, assignments of land revenue, and some historians argue there were too few good jagirs for a growing nobility, a “jagirdari crisis” [C]. Between 1707 and 1719 there were several succession wars and a run of short reigns [E], while the Marathas, Sikhs, Jats and others asserted power across the empire [E].

Governors founded near-independent states: [[Hyderabad|place]] under the Nizam from 1724, then [[Bengal|place]] and [[Awadh|place]] [E]. In 1739 [[Nadir Shah|person]] sacked Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne [E]. The [[East India Company|term]] took control of Bengal after [[Plassey|event]] in 1757 [E], and the dynasty ended in 1857 [E].

Historians such as [[Irfan Habib|person]] stressed an agrarian and fiscal crisis at the centre [L]. Others, including [[Muzaffar Alam|person]] and [[C. A. Bayly|person]], argue that wealth and administration moved to regional states rather than simply collapsing [C].
